high.title: Deep link loads an attacker URL into an authenticated WebView
high.description:
Two findings in this app combine into a single exploitable path: "WebView loads a URL taken from an Intent extra" and "WebView has JavaScript enabled".

Attack path:
1. Attacker sends Intent to WebViewActivity
2. WebViewActivity extracts URL from Intent extra
3. WebViewActivity enables JavaScript
4. WebViewActivity calls loadUrl with the extracted URL
high.impact: The deep link's URL parameter reaches the WebView without a host allowlist, so an attacker picks the page that renders inside the app's trusted UI while it still holds the user's session. Depending on the WebView's settings that means cookie and token theft, local file reads through file://, or script execution via javascript: and data: URLs.
high.recommendation: Parse the incoming URL and compare its host against an exact allowlist. Reject every scheme except https. Do not rely on contains() or startsWith() checks - 'trusted.com' matches 'trusted.com.evil.com'.

high.title: WebView loads a URL taken from an Intent extra
high.description: A WebView load call is fed data that originates from an Intent, so whoever can send that Intent controls what the WebView loads.
high.impact: With a JavaScript bridge or file access enabled on the same WebView, this is the deep-link to WebView chain: attacker content running with the app's bridge privileges.

lines_html: android.webkit.WebView webView = (android.webkit.WebView) findViewById(edu.ksu.cs.benign.R.id.WebView);
android.webkit.WebSettings webSettings = webView.getSettings();
cookieManager.setAcceptCookie(false);
webSettings.setJavaScriptEnabled(true);
webView.loadUrl(getIntent().getStringExtra("url"));

high.recommendation: Validate the URL against an allowlist of exact hosts before loading. Reject javascript:, file: and data: schemes.

low.title: Cleartext traffic permitted and used
low.description: The app targets SDK 27 (which permits cleartext by default) and uses unencrypted HTTP URLs for communication with its backend.
low.impact: Sensitive data transmitted over HTTP can be intercepted or modified by a man-in-the-middle attacker.
low.recommendation: Use HTTPS for all network communication and implement a Network Security Configuration to block cleartext traffic.

reasons: The plain-HTTP address in the code is a development host (private or loopback network), not an endpoint reached over the internet.
warnings: Cleartext is blocked by default from targetSdk 28; confirm the declared target and any network security config.

low.title: WebView has JavaScript enabled
low.description: JavaScript is enabled. On its own this is normal; it is what makes every other WebView weakness on this page exploitable.

lines_html: android.webkit.CookieManager cookieManager = android.webkit.CookieManager.getInstance();
android.webkit.WebView webView = (android.webkit.WebView) findViewById(edu.ksu.cs.benign.R.id.WebView);
android.webkit.WebSettings webSettings = webView.getSettings();
cookieManager.setAcceptCookie(false);
webSettings.setJavaScriptEnabled(true);
webView.loadUrl(getIntent().getStringExtra("url"));

low.recommendation: Disable this setting unless the WebView only ever loads trusted, app-bundled content.

info.title: Application is debuggable in this build
info.description: android:debuggable="true" lets any user with adb attach a debugger to the process, read and modify memory, and inspect application data. The application is marked as debuggable in the manifest. This allows an attacker with ADB access to attach a debugger, explore the app's internal state, and access the app's private data directory using the 'run-as' command.
info.impact: Full runtime access to the app's process and data on any device with adb.
info.recommendation: Remove android:debuggable or set it to "false" for release builds.

reasons: Debuggable release build. A debuggable build is a release-pipeline defect rather than an exploitable flaw - attaching a debugger already requires ADB access to the device. Worth fixing, not worth a severity.

info.title: Missing screen capture protection
info.description: The app does not use FLAG_SECURE to prevent screenshots or screen recordings of its activities.
info.impact: Sensitive information displayed on the screen can be captured by other apps or recorded by the user.
info.recommendation: Set FLAG_SECURE in the window flags for activities displaying sensitive data.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.
Screen contents not protected from capture reaches at most CVSS 3.3 (Low); the vector given scores this finding above anything the class does.
No evidence is provided of sensitive data being displayed on screen that would necessitate capture protection.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.
Lack of certificate pinning is a hardening note and not a vulnerability unless a specific high-value target is identified.

info.title: Private network address 10.0.2.2 shipped in the app
info.description: A private (RFC 1918) address appears in resources/res/values/strings.xml at line 33. It names a development or internal host and grants nothing by itself; it is recorded because it tells a reader about internal infrastructure, or that a development endpoint shipped in the build.
info.impact: None directly. If the app sends requests to it, the cleartext and endpoint findings for that host carry the risk.
info.recommendation: Point release builds at production hosts through build configuration, and leave development addresses out of them.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 27, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise. The app targets Android SDK 27, which misses several security improvements introduced in later versions (e.g., implicit export restrictions, scoped storage).
info.impact: Increases the attack surface by enabling legacy platform behaviors that are insecure by modern standards.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
An SDK level is a platform default, not a vulnerability; it is context for findings where a component is unintentionally exported.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

related_findings.reason: same code line, reported by agent at Informational

reasons: Cleartext permitted by configuration. The flag permits HTTP; it does not show that anything is sent over it. Name a request that actually goes out in cleartext, and what it carries, and this is a genuine finding.
Permitting cleartext via SDK level is a configuration default that only matters if cleartext is actually used, as seen in Cleartext traffic permitted and used.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task.
info.impact: On a device running Android 10 or lower, a malicious app can put a look-alike screen on top of this app's task, phishing credentials or keeping the real app from being shown.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.

reasons: No sensitive activities (e.g., login screens) were identified that would make this phishing risk concrete.

info.title: Task hijacking exposure
info.description: The app uses default task affinity and targets SDK 27, making it potentially susceptible to task hijacking (e.g., StrandHogg) on older Android versions.
info.impact: A malicious app with the same task affinity could potentially overlay its own activities on top of the app's tasks to phish user credentials.
info.recommendation: Set android:taskAffinity to an empty string for activities that do not require a specific task group.

reasons: Client-side protection. Root, emulator, debugger, integrity and pinning checks run on the device they check, so whoever controls that device can hook or patch them. Present, they raise the cost of analysis without stopping it; absent, they expose nothing that was not already the device owner's. Either way this is context, not a vulnerability.
This is a duplicate of Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower.
